rows.measured: Hemolymph thermal hysteresis of up to 5.5 degrees C (freezing point held 5.5 C below the melting point); larvae held 4 weeks at 4 C reached more than 4 C of hysteresis, with a roughly 20-fold rise in thermal hysteresis protein over larvae kept at 22 C.
rows.cite: Graham, Laurie A., Virginia K. Walker, and Peter L. Davies. "Developmental and environmental regulation of antifreeze proteins in the mealworm beetle Tenebrio molitor." *European Journal of Biochemistry* 267, no. 21 (2000): 6452-58. https://doi.org/10.1046/j.1432-1327.2000.01734.x PMID 11029589.
rows.origins: At least twice for fish antifreeze glycoproteins: the Antarctic notothenioid and Arctic cod genes have different progenitors, intron-exon layouts and spacer sequences, so they arose separately. Chen, Liangbiao, Arthur L. DeVries, and Chi-Hing C. Cheng. "Convergent evolution of antifreeze glycoproteins in Antarctic notothenioid fish and Arctic cod." *Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America* 94, no. 8 (1997): 3817-22. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.94.8.3817 PMID 9108061. The beetle protein is a disulfide-bonded beta-helix unrelated to either fish gene, but no phylogeny paper counting insect origins was opened today.
rows.molecule: yes; Tenebrio molitor thermal hysteresis protein (TmAFP, beta-helical antifreeze protein); UniProt O16119 (Thermal hysteresis protein YL-1, Tenebrio molitor), read from the UniProt REST API today. The ice-binding face is the Thr array, shown by steric mutations (Marshall et al., FEBS Letters 529, no. 2-3 (2002): 261-67, https://doi.org/10.1016/s0014-5793(02)03355-0 PMID 12372611).
rows.human: no; not found. The closest work is in other mammals: a tick antifreeze glycoprotein (IAFGP) made transgenic mouse skin resist frostbite (Heisig et al., PLoS One 10, no. 2 (2015): e0116562, https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0116562 PMID 25714402), and antifreeze proteins were delivered into porcine epidermis by silk microneedles (Penney et al., ACS Omega 11, no. 12 (2026): 19023-30, https://doi.org/10.1021/acsomega.5c11565 PMID 41939373).
rows.drug: none found; no agency page was fetched, because no candidate drug based on this protein was named in any paper opened today.
rows.T: T1=1 one gene, a single small secreted protein; T2=1 extracellular, it works in hemolymph and on ice surfaces outside the cell; T3=0 not catalytic, it binds ice crystal faces; T4=0 no human target, its target is ice; T5=0 no human cell or human assay result found; T6=1 small protein, 84 residues, expressible in bacteria in folded active form (PMID 16542851). Scored from the molecule and human columns before any drug search.
rows.N: N1=1 the number is in the abstract of a primary paper opened today; N2=1 the molecule has a UniProt accession read today (O16119); N3=1 a named lab holds the animals and the assay: Departments of Biochemistry and Biology, Queen's University, Kingston, Ontario (Graham, Walker and Davies affiliation on the cited paper), which reared the mealworm larvae and ran the thermal hysteresis measurements.
rows.verified: Opened today: measured (Graham 2000 abstract), origins (Chen 1997 abstract), molecule (UniProt O16119; Marshall 2002 abstract). The mouse and pig papers were opened but are not human. Nothing here rests on a review.

rows.measured: Adding this bacterium's ice-binding protein (FfIBP) to the vitrification and warming solutions raised survival of vitrified mouse metaphase-II oocytes from 75.0% to 89.0%, blastocyst rate per surviving oocyte from 30.7% to 78.0%, and cut DNA double-strand-break-positive oocytes from 65.2% to 30.8%. This is the molecule's effect in a cryopreservation assay, not the organism's own measured freezing tolerance.
rows.cite: Lee, Hyang Heun, Hee Jun Lee, Hak Jun Kim, Jun Hyuck Lee, Yong Ko, Sun Mie Kim, Jung Ryeol Lee, Chang Suk Suh, and Seok Hyun Kim. "Effects of antifreeze proteins on the vitrification of mouse oocytes: comparison of three different antifreeze proteins." *Human Reproduction* 30, no. 9 (2015): 2110-19. https://doi.org/10.1093/humrep/dev170 PMID 26202918.
rows.origins: Ice-binding proteins have arisen more than once in fish alone: Chen, Liangbiao, Arthur L. DeVries, and Chi-Hing C. Cheng. No paper counting origins across bacteria, yeast and fish was opened today.
rows.molecule: yes by name, no by accession; ice-binding protein FfIBP of Flavobacterium frigoris, named in the cited paper. UniProt accession: not found, none was read today for this protein.
rows.human: no; the cited paper states that treatment of human oocytes and embryos with these proteins should be tested before clinical use, so no human result exists there.

rows.measured: Held steady-state torpor at an ambient temperature of -26 degrees C by raising torpid metabolic rate 36-fold over its minimum (measured at 0 C); in a ramped exposure individuals stayed torpid down to -30 C. The temperate comparison species, Callospermophilus lateralis, managed -8 C with a 13.5-fold rise.
rows.cite: Richter, M. M., C. T. Williams, T. N. Lee, O. Toien, G. L. Florant, B. M. Barnes, and C. L. Buck. "Thermogenic capacity at subzero temperatures: how low can a hibernator go?" *Physiological and Biochemical Zoology* 88, no. 1 (2014): 81-89. https://doi.org/10.1086/679591 PMID 25590595.
rows.origins: not found; no phylogeny paper counting independent origins of mammalian hibernation or of deep cold defence was found in this session.
rows.molecule: no; the cited paper reports whole-animal metabolism and names no gene or protein, so there is no accession to read.
rows.human: no; not found for this species. A different hibernator, Ictidomys tridecemlineatus, was used to find cold-tolerance pathways in human iPSC-derived neurons and in cold-stored kidneys (Ou et al., Cell 173, no. 4 (2018): 851-863.e16, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cell.2018.03.010 PMID 29576452), but no molecule from Urocitellus parryii was tested in a human cell.

"A small stress protein acts synergistically with trehalose to confer desiccation tolerance on mammalian cells." *Cryobiology* 51, no. 1 (2005): 15-28. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cryobiol.2005.04.007 PMID 15963489.

rows.measured: The tardigrade-unique DNA-associating protein Dsup, expressed in human cultured cells, cut X-ray-induced DNA damage by about 40% and improved the cells' radiotolerance.
rows.cite: Hashimoto, Takuma, Daiki D. Horikawa, Yuki Saito, Hirokazu Kuwahara, Hiroko Kozuka-Hata, Tadasu Shin-I, Yohei Minakuchi, et al. "Extremotolerant tardigrade genome and improved radiotolerance of human cultured cells by tardigrade-unique protein." *Nature Communications* 7 (2016): 12808. https://doi.org/10.1038/ncomms12808 PMID 27649274.
rows.origins: not found; no phylogeny paper counting independent origins of radiation tolerance was opened today. A second, unrelated route exists in bacteria: Deinococcus radiodurans repairs a genome shattered by 5 kGy of gamma radiation without loss of viability, while 25 kGy leaves frequent genome rearrangements among survivors (Repar, Jelena, Svjetlana Cvjetan, Dea Slade, Miroslav Radman, Davor Zahradka, and Ksenija Zahradka. "RecA protein assures fidelity of DNA repair and genome stability in Deinococcus radiodurans." *DNA Repair* 9, no. 11 (2010): 1151-61. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dnarep.2010.08.003 PMID 20817622), but that paper does not count origins.
rows.molecule: yes; Dsup (damage suppressor protein), gene Dsup / RvY_17224; UniProt P0DOW4 (Damage suppressor protein, Ramazzottius varieornatus), read from the UniProt REST API today.
rows.human: yes; Dsup was expressed in human HEK293 cells and reduced X-ray DNA damage and improved survival in the primary paper above (PMID 27649274), and in human HEK293 cells it also raised survival and cut cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers after UV-C and hydrogen peroxide (Ricci, Claudia, Giulia Riolo, Carlotta Marzocchi, Jlenia Brunetti, Alessandro Pini, and Silvia Cantara. "The Tardigrade Damage Suppressor Protein Modulates Transcription Factor and DNA Repair Genes in Human Cells Treated with Hydroxyl Radicals and UV-C." *Biology* 10, no. 10 (2021): 970. https://doi.org/10.3390/biology10100970 PMID 34681069). Caution from a third primary paper: in cultured rat cortical neurons the same protein caused DNA double-strand breaks and neurotoxicity (Escarcega et al., Molecular and Cellular Neurosciences 125 (2023): 103826, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.mcn.2023.103826 PMID 36858083).
rows.drug: none found; no agency page fetched. No approved agent based on Dsup was named in any paper opened today.

rows.measured: Through hibernation the activation frequency of intracortical bone remodeling fell 75% compared with the active season, while mineral apposition rate per osteon, cortical porosity, bone geometry and whole-bone mechanical properties were unchanged; hibernating femurs were in fact less porous and more mineralised than active ones.
rows.cite: McGee, Meghan E., Aaron J. Maki, Steven E. Johnson, O. Lynne Nelson, Charles T. Robbins, and Seth W. Donahue. "Decreased bone turnover with balanced resorption and formation prevent cortical bone loss during disuse (hibernation) in grizzly bears (Ursus arctos horribilis)." *Bone* 42, no. 2 (2007): 396-404. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bone.2007.10.010 PMID 18037367.

rows.molecule: no; the cited paper measures histomorphometry and mechanics and names no gene product. Cross, Clifford J. Rosen, Robert C. Causey, Caren M. Gundberg, Thomas O. Carpenter, Tai C. Chen, et al. "Investigating the mechanism for maintaining eucalcemia despite immobility and anuria in the hibernating American black bear (Ursus americanus)." *Bone* 49, no. 6 (2011): 1205-12. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bone.2011.08.017 PMID 21893223), but no single molecule was shown to carry the effect, so no accession was read for this row.

rows.measured: In 7 free-ranging female black bears biopsied at den entry and again just before den exit, muscle-fiber number and fiber cross-sectional area in gastrocnemius and biceps femoris were unchanged across the whole denning period, with only a moderate fall in muscle protein concentration. The number is the zero change in fiber cross-sectional area over one denning season in 7 animals; the abstract gives no percentage, so this is a weaker number than the other rows in this block.
rows.cite: Tinker, D. B., H. J. Harlow, and T. D. Beck. "Protein use and muscle-fiber changes in free-ranging, hibernating black bears." *Physiological Zoology* 71, no. 4 (1998): 414-24. https://doi.org/10.1086/515429 PMID 9678502.
rows.origins: not found; no phylogeny paper counting independent origins of atrophy resistance was opened today.
rows.molecule: partly; no molecule in the cited paper. A separate primary paper points at two: serum from hibernating Ursus thibetanus japonicus raised total protein in cultured human myotubes, with lower MuRF1 protein, activated Akt/FOXO3a signalling and higher serum IGF-1 (Miyazaki, Mitsunori, Michito Shimozuru, and Toshio Tsubota. "Supplementing cultured human myotubes with hibernating bear serum results in increased protein content by modulating Akt/FOXO3a signaling." *PLoS One* 17, no. 1 (2022): e0263085. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0263085 PMID 35077510). UniProt read today for the named human target: P05019 (Insulin-like growth factor 1, gene IGF1, Homo sapiens). The active component of bear serum is not identified, so the molecule is not pinned down.
rows.human: yes, but for the serum rather than a single molecule; hibernating bear serum acted on cultured human skeletal muscle myotubes, raising total protein content and lowering MuRF1 through Akt/FOXO3a: Miyazaki et al., *PLoS One* 17, no. 1 (2022): e0263085, https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0263085 PMID 35077510. That paper states the bear and human IGF-1 peptide sequences are identical.
